---
title: "5 Specification of linear economic models"
---

## 5.1 The multiple regression model and goodness-of-fit statistics {#sec-regression}

In earlier sections we have repeatedly used the regression model for trend analysis or for extrapolation for forecasting purposes. The extensive use we make of linear models, not only for time series, calls for a dedicated treatment: on the one hand, to address the questions left unanswered so far and, on the other, to present in a unified and general way the important issue of model specification and of the interpretation of the corresponding estimates.

The file *abitazioni.csv* contains the sale prices (*prezzo*), lot size (*dimensione*), number of bedrooms (*letto*), number of bathrooms (*bagno*) and number of storage rooms (*ripostiglio*) of 546 houses. Assuming the model $Y_{i}=\alpha +\beta X_{i}+\varepsilon_{i}$ for $i=1,...,n$, OLS estimation with the `lm()` function gives the following results.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
abit <- read.csv2("data/abitazioni.csv")
attach(abit)
modrg <- lm(prezzo~dimensione+letto+bagno+ripostiglio)
summary(modrg)
```

### Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from scipy import stats

abit = pd.read_csv("data/abitazioni.csv", sep=";")
modrg = smf.ols("prezzo ~ dimensione + letto + bagno + ripostiglio", data=abit).fit()
print(modrg.summary())
```

### SAS

```sas
proc import datafile="data/abitazioni.csv" out=abit dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;

proc reg data=abit;
  modrg: model prezzo = dimensione letto bagno ripostiglio;
run;
quit;
```
:::

The estimates show that all the variables are significant except the intercept, which in any case takes an implausible negative value. The other estimates are positive, indicating that an increase in the $X$ leads to an increase in the house price $Y$. In particular, if lot size is measured in square metres and price in dollars, we can say that, other things being equal (that is, holding the other explanatory variables fixed), a 1 m² increase in lot size corresponds to an increase in house price of about $5.43. Likewise, with the other explanatory variables held fixed, an extra bedroom raises the house price by $2,825 on average, although the explanatory power of this variable appears less important than that of lot size (its p-value is higher); similar considerations apply to the other estimates. The p-value can be read as the lowest significance level at which the null hypothesis is rejected, which here is the hypothesis that the individual coefficient is zero. In other words, it is very unlikely that lot size has no influence on the prices in our sample and that what we observe is due to chance alone (the p-value is 0.000), whereas the same statement is riskier for the number of bedrooms (the p-value is 0.020).

The *residual standard error* shown in the output is

$$
rse\equiv s=\left(\sum (Y-\hat{Y})^{2}/df\right)^{1/2}
\tag{5.1}
$$

that is, explicitly or more concisely

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
y <- prezzo; ym <- mean(y)
yc <- modrg$fitted
n <- length(y)
u2 <- (y-yc)^2
dof <- n-5
rse <- (sum(u2)/dof)^(0.5); rse
sqrt(deviance(modrg)/df.residual(modrg))
```

### Python

```{python}
y = abit["prezzo"]; ym = y.mean()
yc = modrg.fittedvalues
n = len(y)
dof = n - 5
rse = np.sqrt(((y - yc) ** 2).sum() / dof)
print(rse, np.sqrt(modrg.mse_resid))
```

### SAS

```sas
/* "Root MSE" in the PROC REG output is the residual standard error */
proc reg data=abit outest=est_rg noprint;
  model prezzo = dimensione letto bagno ripostiglio / rsquare adjrsq;
run;
quit;
proc print data=est_rg noobs; var _RMSE_ _RSQ_ _ADJRSQ_; run;
```
:::

Computing the coefficient of determination

$$
R^{2}=rgss/tss
\tag{5.2}
$$

is quite straightforward, where

$$
rgss=\sum (\hat{Y}-\bar{Y})^{2} \quad , \quad tss=\sum (Y-\bar{Y})^{2}
\tag{5.3}
$$

and $tss=rgss+ssr$, with $ssr=\sum (Y-\hat{Y})^{2}$.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
rgss <- sum((yc-ym)^2)
tss <- sum((y-ym)^2)
Rqu <- rgss/tss
Rqu
```

### Python

```{python}
rgss = ((yc - ym) ** 2).sum()
tss = ((y - ym) ** 2).sum()
Rqu = rgss / tss
print(Rqu, modrg.rsquared)
```

### SAS

```sas
/* the sums of squares are in the "Analysis of Variance" table of PROC REG:
   Model = rgss, Error = ssr, Corrected Total = tss */
```
:::

$R^{2}$ measures the share of the total variance of $Y$ that can be explained by $X$ through the linear model; high values indicate a good fit of the model to the observed data.

When using a multiple regression model, however, the coefficient of determination should be adjusted to take into account the number of explanatory variables. Indeed, $R^{2}$ tends to increase simply because variables are added, so the adjustment becomes necessary when comparing linear models with different numbers of explanatory variables. The adjusted $R^{2}$ is

$$
R_{c}^{2}=1-[(1-R^{2})(n-1)/df]
\tag{5.4}
$$

The $F$ statistic, by contrast, tests the significance of the regression as a whole, with null hypothesis $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\beta_{3}=\beta_{4}=0$; it can also be computed from the relationship between $F$ and $R^{2}$.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
Rqa <- 1-((1-Rqu)*(n-1)/dof)
Rqa
mrss <- rgss/4
ssr <- tss-rgss
mssr <- ssr/dof
F <- mrss/mssr
F
Fcrit <- qf(0.05, 4, 541, lower.tail=FALSE)
Fcrit
(Rqu/4)/((1-Rqu)/dof)
```

### Python

```{python}
Rqa = 1 - (1 - Rqu) * (n - 1) / dof
F = (rgss / 4) / ((tss - rgss) / dof)
Fcrit = stats.f.ppf(0.95, 4, 541)
print(Rqa, F, Fcrit, (Rqu / 4) / ((1 - Rqu) / dof))
```

### SAS

```sas
data _null_;
  Fcrit = finv(0.95, 4, 541);   /* critical value of F */
  put Fcrit=;
run;
```
:::

As the p-values show, both the $F$ statistic and the $\beta$ estimates are significant, which implies observed test statistics inside the rejection regions of the null hypothesis.

Given the relationship between $F$ and $R^{2}$, we can also find a critical value for the coefficient of determination under the null hypothesis that $R^{2}$ equals 0

$$
R_{t}^{2}=((k-1)F_{t})/((k-1)F_{t}+(n-k))
\tag{5.5}
$$

where $k$ is the number of parameters of the model, $n$ the number of observations and $F_{t}$ the critical value of the $F$ statistic.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
RqCr <- ((5-1)*Fcrit)/((5-1)*Fcrit+(546-5)); RqCr
```

### Python

```{python}
print(((5 - 1) * Fcrit) / ((5 - 1) * Fcrit + (546 - 5)))
```

### SAS

```sas
data _null_;
  Ft = finv(0.95, 4, 541);
  RqCr = ((5-1)*Ft) / ((5-1)*Ft + (546-5));
  put RqCr=;
run;
```
:::

The coefficient of determination is beyond the critical value; so, at 95% confidence, the null hypothesis $R^{2}=0$ is rejected.

## 5.2 Estimates and confidence intervals in matrix form {#sec-matrix}

As with `summary()`, we could compute the estimated coefficients with their standard errors, Student's t statistics and p-values "by hand", with the following commands; the 95% confidence interval can be obtained in the same way.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
intercetta <- rep(1,n)
xx <- cbind(intercetta, dimensione, letto, bagno, ripostiglio)
xtx <- solve(t(xx)%*%xx)
stime <- xtx%*%t(xx)%*%y
sec <- sqrt(diag(xtx))*rse
tstu <- stime/sec
pvalue <- 2*pt(-abs(tstu), dof)
matrice <- cbind(stime, sec, tstu, pvalue)
colnames(matrice) <- c("stime","errori","test-t","p-value")
round(matrice,3)
tdx <- qt(0.975, dof)
infe <- stime-tdx*sec; supe <- stime+tdx*sec
intervallo <- cbind(infe, supe)
colnames(intervallo) <- c("inferiore","superiore")
round(intervallo,3)
```

### Python

```{python}
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), abit[["dimensione", "letto", "bagno", "ripostiglio"]]])
xtx = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
stime = xtx @ X.T @ y.to_numpy()
sec = np.sqrt(np.diag(xtx)) * rse
tstu = stime / sec
pvalue = 2 * stats.t.cdf(-np.abs(tstu), dof)
tdx = stats.t.ppf(0.975, dof)
matrice = pd.DataFrame({"stime": stime, "errori": sec, "test-t": tstu, "p-value": pvalue,
                        "inferiore": stime - tdx * sec, "superiore": stime + tdx * sec},
                       index=["intercetta", "dimensione", "letto", "bagno", "ripostiglio"])
print(matrice.round(3))
```

### SAS

```sas
proc iml;
  use abit;
  read all var {dimensione letto bagno ripostiglio} into X0;
  read all var {prezzo} into y;
  close abit;
  n = nrow(X0);  X = j(n,1,1) || X0;
  xtx = inv(X`*X);
  stime = xtx*X`*y;
  dof = n - ncol(X);
  rse = sqrt(ssq(y - X*stime)/dof);
  sec = sqrt(vecdiag(xtx))*rse;
  tstu = stime/sec;
  pvalue = 2*cdf("T", -abs(tstu), dof);
  tdx = quantile("T", 0.975, dof);
  matrice = stime || sec || tstu || pvalue || (stime - tdx*sec) || (stime + tdx*sec);
  print matrice[colname={"stime" "errori" "test-t" "p-value" "inferiore" "superiore"}
                rowname={"intercetta" "dimensione" "letto" "bagno" "ripostiglio"} format=12.3];
quit;
```
:::

Or, using the dedicated command:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
confint(modrg)
```

### Python

```{python}
print(modrg.conf_int())
```

### SAS

```sas
proc reg data=abit;
  model prezzo = dimensione letto bagno ripostiglio / clb;   /* clb = confidence intervals */
run;
quit;
```
:::

Note that the confidence interval for the number of bedrooms is rather wide, from a minimum of $438 to a maximum of $5,211; in other words, the marginal effect of $2,825 on house prices for an extra bedroom is imprecise and calls for greater caution in interpretation.

## 5.3 Omitting relevant variables {#sec-omitted}

Let us now estimate house prices as a function of the number of bedrooms only.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
mod1 <- lm(prezzo~letto)
summary(mod1)
```

### Python

```{python}
mod1 = smf.ols("prezzo ~ letto", data=abit).fit()
print(mod1.summary().tables[1], "\nadjusted R2:", mod1.rsquared_adj)
```

### SAS

```sas
proc reg data=abit;
  mod1: model prezzo = letto;
run;
quit;
```
:::

The point estimate is now very different: an extra bedroom would push the house price up by about $13,270. In fact the explanatory power of the model has fallen, because we have excluded variables that are significant both economically and (especially, in this case) statistically (although the two aspects are related); the adjusted coefficient of determination $R_{c}^{2}$ shows the deterioration of the model, from 0.5321 to 0.1327. Such a high marginal effect ($13,270) compared with the full model ($2,825) precisely reflects the omission of important variables; the mistake would be to read the $13,270 as an effect due entirely to the extra bedroom, when an additional bedroom is typical of larger houses, sometimes with more outdoor space, more bathrooms, more storage rooms, etc. Indeed, if *dati* is the data frame containing the variables, the correlations among them reveal a positive interdependence.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
dati <- abit
round(cor(dati),3)
```

### Python

```{python}
print(abit.corr().round(3))
```

### SAS

```sas
proc corr data=abit noprob;
  var prezzo dimensione letto bagno ripostiglio;
run;
```
:::

Omitting relevant explanatory variables biases the estimator $\beta$, and the bias is stronger the closer the relationship between the included and the excluded explanatory variables, since the omitted variables act through their correlation with those included in the model. The solution, however, is not to add as many variables as possible: there is a trade-off between adding variables and complicating the model, with the resulting difficulties of interpretation and sometimes of estimation. Rather, the effort should be to add the variables that the economic literature and the analyst's experience indicate as most important, without losing sight of the advantages of a parsimonious model and accepting the risk of leaving out some important variable anyway; some will slip through regardless, if not through the analyst's error then perhaps because the statistical information is unavailable.

We estimate a new model including only the first two explanatory variables, lot size and number of bedrooms. Lot size is clearly an important variable; through the direct relationship between the two explanatory variables we check the error we would make by excluding *dimensione*.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
modb <- lm(prezzo~dimensione+letto)
summary(modb)
modc <- lm(dimensione~letto)
coef(modc)
1.057e+04 + 6.053e+00 * 446.5
coef(modb)["letto"] + coef(modb)["dimensione"] * coef(modc)["letto"]
```

### Python

```{python}
modb = smf.ols("prezzo ~ dimensione + letto", data=abit).fit()
print(modb.summary().tables[1])
modc = smf.ols("dimensione ~ letto", data=abit).fit()
print(modc.params)
print(modb.params["letto"] + modb.params["dimensione"] * modc.params["letto"])
```

### SAS

```sas
proc reg data=abit;
  modb: model prezzo = dimensione letto;
  modc: model dimensione = letto;
run;
quit;
```
:::

That is, apart from numerical approximation, the regression coefficient of model `mod1`, with only the number of bedrooms explaining house prices, equals the corresponding coefficient of model `modb`, with both *dimensione* and *letto*, plus a bias of $6.053 \cdot 446.5$, given by the product of the coefficient of *dimensione* in `modb` and that of *letto* in the direct relationship between the explanatory variables (model `modc`); this bias vanishes if the correlation between *letto* and *dimensione* is zero.

The opposite risk to excluding important variables is including statistically irrelevant ones. An irrelevant variable in the model generally has a low, but rarely zero, correlation with the other included explanatory variables; however low, this correlation affects the variance of the estimators: it can be shown that including an irrelevant variable does not bias the estimators of the other explanatory variables but increases their variance, and therefore reduces the precision of the estimates.

## 5.4 Multicollinearity {#sec-multicollinearity}

Obviously, everything is correlated with everything. But when the correlation among explanatory variables is too high, the statistical problem of multicollinearity may arise. With multicollinearity the model cannot properly attribute statistical weight to the individual explanatory variables and, in extreme cases, it signals a strong dependence of $Y$ on the $X$, with a high $F$ statistic and a high $R^{2}$, but no statistical significance for the individual explanatory variables; that is, the empirical values of the $t$ statistics are low and fall in the acceptance region of the null hypothesis: an obvious contradiction.

With strong collinearity, a first simple step is to drop the explanatory variables that create statistical redundancy. But what if the variables are indicated by economic theory and their exclusion is justified statistically but not economically? In these cases, which are in fact the majority, the solution is not simple. One could transform the variables, try replacing them with different indicators or combine them into a new variable to replace those causing redundancy, but here too one risks stripping the model of economic meaning.

Let us build two artificial variables with strong collinearity. The dependent variable *prezzo* is correlated with both, and we might find it reasonable to estimate a model including them as explanatory variables.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
var1 <- dimensione
var2 <- log(dimensione)/2
cor(var1, var2)
cor(prezzo, var1); cor(prezzo, var2)
modcor <- lm(prezzo~var1+var2)
round(summary(modcor)$coeff, 4)
```

### Python

```{python}
abit["var1"] = abit["dimensione"]
abit["var2"] = np.log(abit["dimensione"]) / 2
print(abit[["var1", "var2", "prezzo"]].corr().round(4))
modcor = smf.ols("prezzo ~ var1 + var2", data=abit).fit()
print(modcor.summary().tables[1])
```

### SAS

```sas
data abit;
  set abit;
  var1 = dimensione;
  var2 = log(dimensione)/2;
run;
proc corr data=abit noprob; var var1 var2 prezzo; run;
proc reg data=abit;
  modcor: model prezzo = var1 var2 / vif tol;   /* VIF and tolerance */
run;
quit;
```
:::

Note that `var1` (*dimensione*) is not significant; we know that this is not the case:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
round(summary(lm(prezzo~var1))$coeff, 4)
```

### Python

```{python}
print(smf.ols("prezzo ~ var1", data=abit).fit().summary().tables[1])
```

### SAS

```sas
proc reg data=abit;
  model prezzo = var1;
run;
quit;
```
:::

The model `modcor` with both explanatory variables cannot attribute to them their proper role in explaining price, precisely because they are strongly correlated: both the estimated coefficient and its statistical significance are distorted.

A quick way to see whether the correlation among the explanatory variables is dangerously high is the statistic

$$
VIF_{j}=1/(1-R_{j}^{2})
\tag{5.6}
$$

where $R_{j}^{2}$ is the coefficient of determination of the model in which the $j$-th explanatory variable is regressed on the others. The VIF follows an empirical rule whereby, if $VIF_{j}>10$ (corresponding to an $R^{2}$ above 0.90), $X_{j}$ is considered highly correlated with the remaining explanatory variables. Since the *VIF* ranges from 1 (no collinearity) to infinity, its reciprocal is sometimes preferred

$$
TOL=1/VIF
\tag{5.7}
$$

known as tolerance; it ranges from 0 (greatest collinearity) to 1 (least collinearity). For our example

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
r <- cor(var1, var2)
vif <- 1/(1-(r^2)); tol <- 1/vif; vif; tol
```

### Python

```{python}
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor

Xv = sm.add_constant(abit[["var1", "var2"]])
vif = variance_inflation_factor(Xv.to_numpy(), 1)
print(vif, 1 / vif)
```

### SAS

```sas
/* VIF and TOL are already in the PROC REG output with the options / vif tol (see above) */
```
:::

which signals a strong risk of multicollinearity.

Note, however, that time-series data tend to be correlated more easily than cross-section data; we will return to this later, but it should be stressed straight away that strong correlation is not always a bad thing. For example, the autoregressive model introduced in the previous chapter, like the distributed-lag model, often shows symptoms of multicollinearity. Nevertheless, strong correlation among the explanatory variables (within certain limits) is not a problem if we are not specifically interested in the coefficient estimates but are looking for a model that fits the data reasonably well and provides a satisfactory short-term forecast.

## 5.5 Centred and standardised variables {#sec-standardised}

It may sometimes be useful to estimate the coefficients after subtracting the means from the variables or after standardising them. We again use the data in *abitazioni.csv*, taking house price, lot size and number of bedrooms.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
nor <- lm(prezzo~dimensione+letto)
pre <- prezzo-mean(prezzo)
dim <- dimensione-mean(dimensione)
let <- letto-mean(letto); med <- lm(pre~dim+let)
pss <- pre/sd(prezzo); dss <- dim/sd(dimensione)
lss <- let/sd(letto); sta <- lm(pss~dss+lss)
round(summary(nor)$coeff,3); round(summary(med)$coeff,3); round(summary(sta)$coeff,3)
detach(abit)
```

### Python

```{python}
v = abit[["prezzo", "dimensione", "letto"]]
nor = smf.ols("prezzo ~ dimensione + letto", data=v).fit()
med = smf.ols("prezzo ~ dimensione + letto", data=v - v.mean()).fit()
sta = smf.ols("prezzo ~ dimensione + letto", data=(v - v.mean()) / v.std()).fit()
for m in (nor, med, sta):
    print(m.params.round(3).to_dict())
```

### SAS

```sas
/* the stb option of PROC REG gives the standardised ("beta") estimates directly */
proc reg data=abit;
  model prezzo = dimensione letto / stb;
run;
quit;
```
:::

Three sets of estimates are reported. The first comes from the standard model and the second from the variables transformed by subtracting their means: note that in the second set the intercept becomes zero while the $\beta$ do not change at all. In the third set the intercept is again zero, but standardising the variables gives "beta" estimates of the coefficients, which do not depend on the units of the original variables. So, if we wanted to compare the importance of the explanatory variables in influencing house prices, the second set of estimates would be misleading, because the corresponding $X$ are measured in different units; by contrast, since the variables in the third set are standardised, we can say that a one-standard-unit change in *dss* causes a reaction in standardised prices about 68% larger than *lss* (0.491/0.292=1.68).

## 5.6 Dummy variables in regression {#sec-dummy-regression}

We introduced dummy variables for classical time series when specifying the seasonal component. We now generalise the use of these special variables in multiple regression models.

The file *case.csv* contains further information on our 546 houses; besides the price, there are now 5 dummy variables taking the value 0 or 1 for the absence or presence of: a driveway (*accesso*), a games room (*giochi*), a cellar (*cantina*), gas heating (*gas*) and air conditioning (*clima*). We assume that the presence or absence of these features may influence house prices. For simplicity, we focus on the OLS estimates of the model with only the first two dummies as regressors.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
case <- read.csv2("data/case.csv")
attach(case)
dum <- lm(prezzo~accesso+giochi)
dum$coeff[1]+dum$coeff[2]*0+dum$coeff[3]*0
dum$coeff[1]+dum$coeff[2]*1+dum$coeff[3]*0
dum$coeff[1]+dum$coeff[2]*0+dum$coeff[3]*1
dum$coeff[1]+dum$coeff[2]*1+dum$coeff[3]*1
```

### Python

```{python}
case = pd.read_csv("data/case.csv", sep=";")
dum = smf.ols("prezzo ~ accesso + giochi", data=case).fit()
combinazioni = pd.DataFrame({"accesso": [0, 1, 0, 1], "giochi": [0, 0, 1, 1]})
print(dum.predict(combinazioni).round(2).to_numpy())
```

### SAS

```sas
proc import datafile="data/case.csv" out=case dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
proc glm data=case;
  model prezzo = accesso giochi / solution;
  estimate "no driveway, no games room" intercept 1;
  estimate "driveway only"           intercept 1 accesso 1;
  estimate "games room only"            intercept 1 giochi 1;
  estimate "both"               intercept 1 accesso 1 giochi 1;
run;
quit;
```
:::

The first result is the average price of houses with neither a driveway nor a games room ($47,099), the second that of houses with a driveway only ($68,258), the third that of houses with a games room only ($63,122) and, finally, the fourth that of houses with both ($84,282). Note straight away that the choice of coding 0 rather than 1 is arbitrary: 0 is logically used for absence and 1 for presence of the feature, but we could swap them without changing anything for interpretation.

Dummy variables make several specifications possible; for example (for ease of notation without subscripts and random error term):

a) as in the previous case, with effects on the intercept only: $Y=\alpha +cX+\beta D$
b) with effects only on the strength of the relationship between $Y$ and $X$: $Y=\alpha +cX+\beta XD$
c) with effects on both the intercept and the slope: $Y=\alpha +cX+\beta D+\gamma XD$

Still using *case.csv*, we estimate the last model (c) with *dimensione* and *clima*.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
dimcli <- dimensione*clima
modwid <- lm(prezzo~dimensione+clima+dimcli)
round(summary(modwid)$coef, 4)
```

### Python

```{python}
case["dimcli"] = case["dimensione"] * case["clima"]
modwid = smf.ols("prezzo ~ dimensione + clima + dimcli", data=case).fit()
print(modwid.summary().tables[1])
```

### SAS

```sas
data case; set case; dimcli = dimensione*clima; run;
proc reg data=case;
  modwid: model prezzo = dimensione clima dimcli;
run;
quit;
```
:::

It follows that the mere presence of air conditioning does not significantly change house prices (p-value 0.1703), but it increases the effect of lot size (*dimensione* and *clima* interact through their product *dimcli*). Without air conditioning, a 1 m² increase in lot size raises the average house price by $5.02, but with air conditioning the increase is 5.02+2.25=$7.27 per square metre.

The t statistic for *clima* would suggest dropping it from the model. The new estimate is therefore:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
modnid <- lm(prezzo~dimensione+dimcli)
round(summary(modnid)$coef, 4)
```

### Python

```{python}
modnid = smf.ols("prezzo ~ dimensione + dimcli", data=case).fit()
print(modnid.summary().tables[1])
```

### SAS

```sas
proc reg data=case;
  modnid: model prezzo = dimensione dimcli;
run;
quit;
```
:::

## 5.7 Parameter restrictions and the F test {#sec-restrictions}

The $F$ test is particularly useful for assessing specific restrictions on the parameters. Suppose we want to check whether the coefficients of *dimensione* and *dimcli* can be considered different only by chance. Then $Y=\alpha +\beta_{1}X_{1}+\beta_{2}X_{2}+e$ is the extended model, while $Y=\alpha +\beta_{1}(X_{1}+X_{2})+e$ is the restricted model to be tested (now there is a single $\beta$). Since

$$
\begin{gathered}F=((rsum-usum)/m)/(usum/(n-k))\equiv \\ \equiv ((r_{u}^{2}-r_{r}^{2})/m)/((1-r_{u}^{2})/(n-k))\end{gathered}
\tag{5.8}
$$

where $rsum$ is the residual sum of squares of the restricted model and $usum$ that of the unrestricted (or extended) model, with $m$ the number of restrictions and $k$ the number of parameters of the extended model, we have

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
n <- nrow(case)
riduz <- dimensione+dimcli
modris <- lm(prezzo~riduz)
round(summary(modris)$coeff, 4)
usum <- anova(modnid)$Sum[3]
rsum <- anova(modris)$Sum[2]
Frestr <- ((rsum-usum)/1)/(usum/(n-3))
Frestr
smodnid <- summary(modnid)
smodris <- summary(modris)
ru <- smodnid$r.square
rr <- smodris$r.square
((ru-rr)/1)/((1-ru)/(n-3))
```

### Python

```{python}
n = len(case)
case["riduz"] = case["dimensione"] + case["dimcli"]
modris = smf.ols("prezzo ~ riduz", data=case).fit()
print(modris.params)
usum, rsum = modnid.ssr, modris.ssr
Frestr = ((rsum - usum) / 1) / (usum / (n - 3))
print(Frestr, ((modnid.rsquared - modris.rsquared) / 1) / ((1 - modnid.rsquared) / (n - 3)))
```

### SAS

```sas
/* the restriction beta(dimensione) = beta(dimcli) is tested
   directly with the TEST statement of PROC REG */
proc reg data=case;
  model prezzo = dimensione dimcli;
  uguali: test dimensione = dimcli;
run;
quit;
```
:::

The result leads, albeit narrowly, to rejecting the null hypothesis of equal coefficients at the 95% confidence level.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
qf(0.95, 1, n-3)
pf(Frestr, 1, n-3, lower.tail=FALSE)
```

### Python

```{python}
print(stats.f.ppf(0.95, 1, n - 3), stats.f.sf(Frestr, 1, n - 3))
print(modnid.f_test("dimensione = dimcli"))
```

### SAS

```sas
data _null_;
  Fcrit = finv(0.95, 1, 546-3);
  put Fcrit=;
run;
```
:::

Note the use of `anova()` to obtain easily the residual sum of squares of the estimated model. For `modnid` we obtain the table below; from the sums of squares and the degrees of freedom it is easy to get the mean squares and the $F$ statistics for testing the significance of the terms of the model.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
anid <- anova(modnid)
anid
anid$Sum # sums = Sum Sq
anid$Sum/anid$Df # means = Mean Sq
anid$Mean[1]/anid$Mean[3]
anid$Mean[2]/anid$Mean[3]
```

### Python

```{python}
# sequential (type I) ANOVA table, like R's anova()
print(sm.stats.anova_lm(modnid, typ=1))
```

### SAS

```sas
/* PROC GLM reports sequential sums of squares (Type I SS), like R's anova() */
proc glm data=case;
  model prezzo = dimensione dimcli / ss1;
run;
quit;
```
:::

To compare the two models more easily, we could also have written

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
anova(modris, modnid)
```

### Python

```{python}
print(sm.stats.anova_lm(modris, modnid))
```

### SAS

```sas
/* equivalent: the TEST statement shown above */
```
:::

The $F$ test is also useful for testing the structural stability of the coefficients of a model estimated over two different time periods, in two different areas or on two different groups of cases (for example, less and more affluent consumers). This particular test statistic is known as the Chow test

$$
\begin{gathered}F_{Chow}=\left((rsum-(usum_{a}+usum_{b}))/k\right)/ \\ \left((usum_{a}+usum_{b})/(n_{a}+n_{b}-2k)\right)\sim F_{k,(n_{a}+n_{b}-2k)}\end{gathered}
\tag{5.9}
$$

where $k$ is the number of parameters, $rsum$ is the residual sum of squares of the restricted model with structural stability (a single model for all observations), while $usum_{a}$ and $usum_{b}$ are the corresponding sums for the unrestricted models, estimated separately for the two groups ($a$ and $b$) of observations.

```{r}
#| include: false
detach(case)
```

## 5.8 The Chow test and structural stability {#sec-chow}

We load the data in *redditousa.csv* on US saving (*risparmio*) and disposable income (*reddito*) from 1970 to 1995. We want to check whether a structural break in the linear saving function occurred between 1981 and 1982. We estimate a first model for 1970-1981, a second for 1982-1995 and a third for the whole period 1970-1995.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
usa <- read.csv2("data/redditousa.csv")
attach(usa)
t(anno)
ante <- lm(risparmio[1:12]~reddito[1:12])
post <- lm(risparmio[13:26]~reddito[13:26])
tutto <- lm(risparmio~reddito)
ant <- summary(ante); pos <- summary(post)
tut <- summary(tutto)
round(ant$coeff,3); round(pos$coeff,3); round(tut$coeff,3)
usuma <- anova(ante)$Sum[2]; usumb <- anova(post)$Sum[2]
rsum <- anova(tutto)$Sum[2]
Fchow <- ((rsum-(usuma+usumb))/2)/((usuma+usumb)/(12+14-2*2))
Fchow
round(pf(Fchow, 2, 22, lower.tail=FALSE), 5)
```

### Python

```{python}
usa = pd.read_csv("data/redditousa.csv", sep=";", decimal=",")
ante = smf.ols("risparmio ~ reddito", data=usa.iloc[:12]).fit()
post = smf.ols("risparmio ~ reddito", data=usa.iloc[12:]).fit()
tutto = smf.ols("risparmio ~ reddito", data=usa).fit()
for m in (ante, post, tutto):
    print(m.params.round(3).to_dict())
Fchow = ((tutto.ssr - (ante.ssr + post.ssr)) / 2) / ((ante.ssr + post.ssr) / (12 + 14 - 2 * 2))
print(Fchow, round(stats.f.sf(Fchow, 2, 22), 5))
```

### SAS

```sas
proc import datafile="data/redditousa.csv" out=usa dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
/* PROC AUTOREG runs the Chow test for a break after the given observation */
proc autoreg data=usa;
  model risparmio = reddito / chow=(13);
run;
```
:::

So the null hypothesis of structural stability of the coefficients over the whole period 1970-1995 is rejected.

Note that the Chow test requires the error variance to be the same in the two models. Let us check whether this is the case.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
Fvar <- (pos$sigma^2)/(ant$sigma^2)
Fvar
round(pf(Fvar, 12, 10, lower.tail=FALSE), 4)
```

### Python

```{python}
Fvar = post.mse_resid / ante.mse_resid
print(Fvar, round(stats.f.sf(Fvar, 12, 10), 4))
```

### SAS

```sas
proc reg data=usa outest=s_ante noprint; where anno <= 1981; model risparmio = reddito; run;
proc reg data=usa outest=s_post noprint; where anno >= 1982; model risparmio = reddito; run;
quit;
data _null_;
  merge s_ante(keep=_RMSE_ rename=(_RMSE_=s_a)) s_post(keep=_RMSE_ rename=(_RMSE_=s_p));
  Fvar = s_p**2 / s_a**2;
  p = 1 - probf(Fvar, 12, 10);
  put Fvar= p=;
run;
```
:::

This suggests rejecting the null hypothesis of equal variances, and hence caution in using the Chow test.

Another way of testing for structural stability is to use dummy variables, equal to 0 from 1970 to 1981 and 1 from 1982 to 1995.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
d1 <- rep(NA,26)
d1[1:12] <- 0
d1[13:26] <- 1
d1x <- d1*reddito
modum <- lm(risparmio~reddito+d1+d1x)
summary(modum)
```

### Python

```{python}
usa["d1"] = (usa["anno"] >= 1982).astype(int)
usa["d1x"] = usa["d1"] * usa["reddito"]
modum = smf.ols("risparmio ~ reddito + d1 + d1x", data=usa).fit()
print(modum.summary().tables[1])
```

### SAS

```sas
data usa;
  set usa;
  d1 = (anno >= 1982);
  d1x = d1*reddito;
run;
proc reg data=usa;
  modum: model risparmio = reddito d1 d1x;
run;
quit;
```
:::

The estimates, except the intercept, are all significant. For 1970-1981, with the dummy equal to 0, we have the first two coefficients, while for 1982-1995 (dummy equal to 1) we have the sums below.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
modum$coeff[1]; modum$coeff[2]
modum$coeff[1]+modum$coeff[3]; modum$coeff[2]+modum$coeff[4]
```

### Python

```{python}
b = modum.params
print(b["Intercept"], b["reddito"])
print(b["Intercept"] + b["d1"], b["reddito"] + b["d1x"])
```

### SAS

```sas
proc glm data=usa;
  model risparmio = reddito d1 d1x / solution;
  estimate "intercept 1982-95" intercept 1 d1 1;
  estimate "slope 1982-95"   reddito 1 d1x 1;
run;
quit;
```
:::

Importantly, the coefficients are almost identical to those of the separate models, where the estimates have 10 and 12 degrees of freedom, whereas with the two dummies we have 22.

## 5.9 Dummies and models without intercept {#sec-no-intercept}

This also allows a further remark on the use of dummy variables. Suppose we are interested only in the level of saving, and hence in the effect of the historical period on it, regardless of income. Consistently with what we have seen, we should introduce a single dummy, equal for example to 0 between 1970 and 1981 and 1 between 1982 and 1995; we cannot introduce two dummies, as that would cause perfect multicollinearity. In fact we can get around this problem by not including the intercept.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
d1 <- rep(NA,26); d2 <- rep(NA,26)
d1[1:12] <- 0; d1[13:26] <- 1
d2[1:12] <- 1; d2[13:26] <- 0
modd <- lm(risparmio~d1+d2)
summary(modd)$coeff
modint <- lm(risparmio~d1+d2-1)
summary(modint)$coeff
mean(risparmio[1:12])
mean(risparmio[13:26])
```

### Python

```{python}
usa["d2"] = 1 - usa["d1"]
# with an intercept and two dummies X is singular: estimate the model without intercept
modint = smf.ols("risparmio ~ d1 + d2 - 1", data=usa).fit()
print(modint.params)
print(usa.groupby("d1")["risparmio"].mean())
```

### SAS

```sas
data usa; set usa; d2 = 1 - d1; run;
proc reg data=usa;
  modd:   model risparmio = d1 d2;           /* SAS reports the linear dependence */
  modint: model risparmio = d1 d2 / noint;   /* model without intercept */
run;
quit;
```
:::

In the model with an intercept, the coefficient of *d2* is not defined because of the singularity, and the sum of the intercept and the estimated coefficient of *d1* equals 209.78. Without the intercept, the coefficients of the two dummies are exactly the average saving in the two periods.

Note that models without an intercept require particular care in interpretation compared with standard models, not least because some statistics (for example $R^{2}$) behave unusually.

## 5.10 Residual diagnostics {#sec-diagnostics}

Let us go back to the model `modum` and use `plot()` to obtain some diagnostics (Figure 5.1). The first `par()` instruction tells **R** to arrange the plots in two columns and two rows within a single graphics device; the second `par()` restores the default layout, while `plot()` draws the four basic diagnostic plots.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 5.1 – Diagnostic plots of the model modum"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7
par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(modum)
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

### Python

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 5.1 – Diagnostic plots of the model modum"
#| results: hide
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

infl = modum.get_influence()
rst = infl.resid_studentized_internal
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(7, 7))
ax[0, 0].scatter(modum.fittedvalues, modum.resid, facecolors="none", edgecolors="black")
ax[0, 0].axhline(0, linestyle=":", color="grey"); ax[0, 0].set_title("Residuals vs Fitted")
sm.qqplot(rst, line="45", ax=ax[0, 1]); ax[0, 1].set_title("Normal Q-Q")
ax[1, 0].scatter(modum.fittedvalues, np.sqrt(np.abs(rst)), facecolors="none", edgecolors="black")
ax[1, 0].set_title("Scale-Location")
ax[1, 1].scatter(infl.hat_matrix_diag, rst, facecolors="none", edgecolors="black")
ax[1, 1].set_title("Residuals vs Leverage")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### SAS

```sas
/* PROC REG produces the diagnostic panel automatically (ODS Graphics) */
ods graphics on;
proc reg data=usa plots=diagnostics;
  model risparmio = reddito d1 d1x;
run;
quit;
```
:::

The four plots of Figure 5.1 are easy to interpret, with evidence of anomalies in cases 15, 23, 25 and, partly, 12. Recall that the standardised residual is $r_{i}=\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}/(\hat{\sigma}\sqrt{1-h_{ii}})$, where the $h_{ii}$ (leverage of the $i$-th observation) are the elements on the main diagonal of the matrix $H=X(X'X)^{-1}X'$. The Jarque-Bera test of normality of the residuals is also useful here

$$
JB=n(S^{2}/6+(K-3)^{2}/24)
\tag{5.10}
$$

with $S$ a measure of skewness (0 for the Normal) and $K$ a measure of kurtosis (3 for the Normal). The JB statistic is asymptotically distributed as $\chi_{(2)}^{2}$. Hence,

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
ee <- resid(modum)
m3 <- mean((ee-mean(ee))^3); S <- m3/(sd(ee)^3)
m4 <- mean((ee-mean(ee))^4); K <- m4/(sd(ee)^4)
S; K
n <- 26
JB <- n*((S^2)/6 + ((K-3)^2)/24)
JB
pchisq(JB, 2, lower.tail=FALSE)
detach(usa)
```

### Python

```{python}
ee = modum.resid
S = np.mean((ee - ee.mean()) ** 3) / ee.std() ** 3      # pandas std() uses n-1, like R's sd()
K = np.mean((ee - ee.mean()) ** 4) / ee.std() ** 4
JB = 26 * (S ** 2 / 6 + (K - 3) ** 2 / 24)
print(S, K, JB, stats.chi2.sf(JB, 2))
```

### SAS

```sas
/* the normal option of PROC AUTOREG computes the Jarque-Bera test on the residuals */
proc autoreg data=usa;
  model risparmio = reddito d1 d1x / normal;
run;
```
:::

The null hypothesis of normality of the residuals cannot be rejected, although the test should be applied for sufficiently large $n$.

## 5.11 Functional form: the MWD test {#sec-mwd}

A typical issue in model specification is the choice of functional form. In most cases the alternative is between a linear and a log-linear form, and generally economic theory itself or the analyst's specific interests lead to one or the other. In some cases the MacKinnon, White and Davidson (MWD) test helps guide the choice.

We load the data in *rose.csv* on quintals of roses sold, the price of the main variety (*prvar1*) and the price of a substitute flower, the carnation (*prvar2*). We estimate the linear and the log-linear model, adding the variables *z1* and *z2* as specified below.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
rosedf <- read.csv2("data/rose.csv")
attach(rosedf)
mo1 <- lm(rose~prvar1+prvar2)
mo2 <- lm(log(rose)~log(prvar1)+log(prvar2))
z1 <- log(fitted(mo1))-fitted(mo2)
z2 <- exp(fitted(mo2))-fitted(mo1)
mod1e <- lm(rose~prvar1+prvar2+z1)
mod2e <- lm(log(rose)~log(prvar1)+log(prvar2)+z2)
round(summary(mod1e)$coeff,3); round(summary(mod2e)$coeff,3)
```

### Python

```{python}
rosedf = pd.read_csv("data/rose.csv", sep=";", decimal=",")
mo1 = smf.ols("rose ~ prvar1 + prvar2", data=rosedf).fit()
mo2 = smf.ols("np.log(rose) ~ np.log(prvar1) + np.log(prvar2)", data=rosedf).fit()
rosedf["z1"] = np.log(mo1.fittedvalues) - mo2.fittedvalues
rosedf["z2"] = np.exp(mo2.fittedvalues) - mo1.fittedvalues
mod1e = smf.ols("rose ~ prvar1 + prvar2 + z1", data=rosedf).fit()
mod2e = smf.ols("np.log(rose) ~ np.log(prvar1) + np.log(prvar2) + z2", data=rosedf).fit()
print(mod1e.summary().tables[1]); print(mod2e.summary().tables[1])
```

### SAS

```sas
proc import datafile="data/rose.csv" out=rosedf dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
data rosedf;
  set rosedf;
  lrose = log(rose); lp1 = log(prvar1); lp2 = log(prvar2);
run;
proc reg data=rosedf noprint;
  model rose = prvar1 prvar2;  output out=r1 p=fit1;
run;
proc reg data=r1 noprint;
  model lrose = lp1 lp2;       output out=r2 p=fit2;
run;
quit;
data r2; set r2; z1 = log(fit1) - fit2; z2 = exp(fit2) - fit1; run;
proc reg data=r2;
  mod1e: model rose  = prvar1 prvar2 z1;
  mod2e: model lrose = lp1 lp2 z2;
run;
quit;
```
:::

*z1* and *z2* are not significant, but the first has a much higher p-value than the second. The null hypotheses they represent concern the linear form of the model for *z1* and the log-linear form for *z2*; so, although both alternatives seem admissible, the high p-value of *z1* recommends the linear form, and hence model `mo1`, over the log-linear form of `mo2`.

## 5.12 The likelihood-ratio test {#sec-lr}

To check whether an explanatory variable can be dropped from the model without significantly worsening it, the likelihood-ratio test can also be used. We take the linear model `mo1`, re-estimate it without *prvar2* (`mo3`) and extract the value of the log-likelihood function, which we compare using an (asymptotic) approximation to a $\chi^{2}$ with 1 degree of freedom (there is 1 restriction).

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
ll1 <- logLik(mo1)
mo3 <- lm(rose~prvar1)
ll3 <- logLik(mo3)
ll1; ll3
lambda <- 2*(ll1[1]-ll3[1])
lambda
pchisq(lambda, 1, lower.tail=FALSE)
detach(rosedf)
```

### Python

```{python}
mo3 = smf.ols("rose ~ prvar1", data=rosedf).fit()
lam = 2 * (mo1.llf - mo3.llf)
print(mo1.llf, mo3.llf, lam, stats.chi2.sf(lam, 1))
```

### SAS

```sas
/* PROC MIXED (maximum likelihood) reports -2 log-likelihood */
proc mixed data=rosedf method=ml;
  model rose = prvar1 prvar2 / solution;
run;
proc mixed data=rosedf method=ml;
  model rose = prvar1 / solution;
run;
/* lambda = difference between the two "-2 Log Likelihood" values */
```
:::

The null hypothesis is therefore rejected, and the restricted model `mo3` is rejected in favour of `mo1`.

## 5.13 Heteroscedasticity {#sec-heteroscedasticity}

When estimating linear models, a condition that is often not met is homoscedasticity, that is, the assumption of constant variance. The error variance may not be constant for various reasons, for example because of an incorrectly specified functional form, the presence of outliers, etc. With heteroscedasticity the estimators are unbiased and consistent but not efficient. One way of dealing with the problem is to use generalised least squares (GLS), weighting, for example, the observations in inverse proportion to the size of the variance (weighted least squares, WLS).

There are several techniques and tests for detecting heteroscedasticity; one of them is the Goldfeld-Quandt test, which assumes that the variance is positively related to a specific explanatory variable.

To run the test we assume a simple model with a single explanatory variable and load the data in *consusa.csv* on the income (*reddito*) and consumption (*consumo*) of 30 US households. We sort the data by the explanatory variable and, dropping $c$ central observations, estimate one model for the first part of the observations and one for the rest, then compare the residual sums of squares with an $F_{(n-c-2k)/2,(n-c-2k)/2}$ test.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
tabella <- read.csv2("data/consusa.csv")
attach(tabella)
tabord <- tabella[order(reddito),]
modet1 <- lm(tabord$consumo[1:13]~tabord$reddito[1:13])
modet2 <- lm(tabord$consumo[(30-13+1):30]~tabord$reddito[(30-13+1):30])
rss1 <- anova(modet1)$Sum[2]
rss2 <- anova(modet2)$Sum[2]
lam <- (rss2/11)/(rss1/11)
lam
qf(0.95, 11, 11)
```

### Python

```{python}
tabella = pd.read_csv("data/consusa.csv", sep=";")
tabord = tabella.sort_values("reddito").reset_index(drop=True)
modet1 = smf.ols("consumo ~ reddito", data=tabord.iloc[:13]).fit()
modet2 = smf.ols("consumo ~ reddito", data=tabord.iloc[17:]).fit()
lam = (modet2.ssr / 11) / (modet1.ssr / 11)
print(lam, stats.f.ppf(0.95, 11, 11))
```

### SAS

```sas
proc import datafile="data/consusa.csv" out=tabella dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
proc sort data=tabella out=tabord; by reddito; run;
data tabord; set tabord; oss = _n_; run;
proc reg data=tabord outest=gq1 noprint; where oss <= 13; model consumo = reddito; run;
proc reg data=tabord outest=gq2 noprint; where oss >= 18; model consumo = reddito; run;
quit;
data _null_;
  merge gq1(keep=_RMSE_ rename=(_RMSE_=s1)) gq2(keep=_RMSE_ rename=(_RMSE_=s2));
  lam = s2**2 / s1**2;    /* same degrees of freedom (11) in the two groups */
  Fcrit = finv(0.95, 11, 11);
  put lam= Fcrit=;
run;
```
:::

The null hypothesis is rejected, so the data show significant heteroscedasticity.

Many other tests exist in the literature; White's test is among the most general. It is based on an auxiliary regression of the squared residuals of the model on the regressors, their squares and their cross-products; the test statistic is the coefficient of determination of the auxiliary regression multiplied by the number of observations, and is asymptotically distributed as a $\chi^{2}$ with degrees of freedom equal to the number of regressors in the auxiliary regression. Hence

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
modwh <- lm(consumo~reddito)
reddito2 <- reddito^2
u2 <- (residuals(modwh))^2
modu2 <- lm(u2~reddito+reddito2)
raux <- summary(modu2)$r.squared
white <- 30*raux
white
pchisq(white, 2, lower.tail=FALSE)
detach(tabella)
```

### Python

```{python}
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import het_white

modwh = smf.ols("consumo ~ reddito", data=tabella).fit()
white, pval, _, _ = het_white(modwh.resid, modwh.model.exog)
print(white, pval)
```

### SAS

```sas
/* the spec option of PROC REG runs White's test */
proc reg data=tabella;
  model consumo = reddito / spec;
run;
quit;
```
:::

At 95% confidence the null hypothesis of homoscedasticity is accepted (narrowly): note that the conclusions of the last two tests contradict each other. If heteroscedasticity is present, there are reweighting techniques that help reduce its consequences, including the so-called White procedure, run by default by most software; we will not go into this further.

## 5.14 Autocorrelation of the residuals {#sec-autocorrelation}

Another common violation of the basic assumptions in estimating a model is autocorrelation of the residuals; it appears over time in time series, across space in cross-section data, or both in more complex situations. The last two cases call for a more detailed treatment that is beyond our scope, but we can give some examples of serial autocorrelation.

If the model can be written as $Y_{t}=\alpha +\beta_{1}X_{1}+\beta_{2}X_{2}+u_{t}$, where $u_{t}$ is not the classical white noise $\varepsilon_{t}$ but a disturbance correlated with itself over time, then in the simplest case we can write

$$
u_{t}=\rho u_{t-1}+\varepsilon_{t}
\tag{5.11}
$$

which is very reminiscent of a first-order autoregressive model, $AR(1)$; $\rho$ is called the first-order autocorrelation coefficient. Of course the dependence of the errors over time could follow a more complex structure with a higher lag, but in most cases the first-order assumption is satisfactory. If we used OLS with serial autocorrelation (as with heteroscedasticity), the estimators would be unbiased and consistent but not efficient.

We load the data in *salari.csv* on hourly wages (*salari*) and hourly productivity (*produtt*) in US industry between 1959 and 1998, and estimate a log-linear model.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
sal <- read.csv2("data/salari.csv")
attach(sal)
modsal <- lm(log(salari)~log(produtt))
summary(modsal)
```

### Python

```{python}
sal = pd.read_csv("data/salari.csv", sep=";", decimal=",")
modsal = smf.ols("np.log(salari) ~ np.log(produtt)", data=sal).fit()
print(modsal.summary())
```

### SAS

```sas
proc import datafile="data/salari.csv" out=sal dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
data sal; set sal; ls = log(salari); lp = log(produtt); run;
proc reg data=sal;
  modsal: model ls = lp / dw;   /* dw = Durbin-Watson statistic */
  output out=res_sal r=u;
run;
quit;
```
:::

We plot the residuals appropriately (Figures 5.2 and 5.3).

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 5.2 – Residuals over time"
u <- residuals(modsal)
plot(u, main="Residuals over time")
abline(h=0)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 5.2 – Residuals over time"
#| results: hide
u = modsal.resid.to_numpy()
plt.figure(figsize=(5, 5))
plt.scatter(np.arange(1, 41), u, facecolors="none", edgecolors="black")
plt.axhline(0, color="black")
plt.title("Residuals over time")
plt.show()
```

### SAS

```sas
data res_sal; set res_sal; t = _n_; u1 = lag(u); run;
proc sgplot data=res_sal;
  title "Residuals over time";
  scatter x=t y=u;
  refline 0 / axis=y;
run;
```
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 5.3 – Autocorrelation of the residuals"
plot(embed(u,2)[,1], embed(u,2)[,2], main="Residuals at time t and t-1")
abline(h=0); abline(v=0)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 5.3 – Autocorrelation of the residuals"
#| results: hide
plt.figure(figsize=(5, 5))
plt.scatter(u[1:], u[:-1], facecolors="none", edgecolors="black")
plt.axhline(0, color="black"); plt.axvline(0, color="black")
plt.title("Residuals at time t and t-1")
plt.show()
```

### SAS

```sas
proc sgplot data=res_sal;
  title "Residuals at time t and t-1";
  scatter x=u y=u1;
  refline 0 / axis=x; refline 0 / axis=y;
run;
```
:::

There is clearly strong positive autocorrelation, whose significance can be assessed with the Durbin-Watson $d$ statistic

$$
d=\sum_{t=2}^{n} (\hat{u}_{t}-\hat{u}_{t-1})^{2}\Big/\sum_{t=1}^{n} \hat{u}_{t}^{2}
\tag{5.12}
$$

It can be shown that, if $\hat{\rho}$ is the autocorrelation coefficient between $\hat{u}_{t}$ and $\hat{u}_{t-1}$,

$$
d\approx 2(1-\hat{\rho})
\tag{5.13}
$$

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
cor(embed(u,2)[,1], embed(u,2)[,2])
ut0 <- embed(u,2)[,1]
ut1 <- embed(u,2)[,2]
dw <- (sum((ut0-ut1)^2))/(sum(u^2))
dw
rho <- cor(ut0, ut1)
dd <- 2*(1-rho)
dd
```

### Python

```{python}
from statsmodels.stats.stattools import durbin_watson

rho = np.corrcoef(u[1:], u[:-1])[0, 1]
print(rho, durbin_watson(u), 2 * (1 - rho))
```

### SAS

```sas
/* PROC AUTOREG reports Durbin-Watson and its p-value */
proc autoreg data=sal;
  model ls = lp / dw=1 dwprob;
run;
```
:::

The critical values of the Durbin-Watson test for $n=40$, $k=2$ and 95% confidence are $d_L=1.44$ and $d_U=1.54$. Since the statistic is below the lower bound, the null hypothesis is rejected in favour of positive autocorrelation. In particular, if

- $0<d<d_{L}$: positive autocorrelation
- $4-d_{L}<d<4$: negative autocorrelation
- $d_{U}<d<4-d_{U}$: no autocorrelation
- $d_{L}\le d\le d_{U}$: inconclusive region
- $4-d_{U}\le d\le 4-d_{L}$: inconclusive region.

Note that the Durbin-Watson statistic is symmetric around $d=2$. Moreover, its correct application requires strict conditions, including the absence of the lagged dependent variable among the explanatory variables.

Finally, note that in some cases strong autocorrelation, as already pointed out for heteroscedasticity, may result from model misspecification rather than from genuine serial dependence in the data.

## 5.15 Correcting for autocorrelation {#sec-ar-correction}

Suppose now that $\rho$ is known and equal to the correlation between $\hat{u}_{t}$ and $\hat{u}_{t-1}$. We estimate a transformed model which, while not eliminating serial autocorrelation entirely, at least reduces it and its consequences for the estimates. The procedure applies OLS to the transformed model, which is equivalent to GLS on the original model $Y=f(X)+u$, that is, $(Y_{t}-\rho Y_{t-1})=\beta_{0}(1-\rho )+\beta_{1}(X_{t}-\rho X_{t-1})+\varepsilon_{t}$, where by construction $\varepsilon_{t}=(u_{t}-\rho u_{t-1})\sim WN$.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
y <- log(salari)
x <- log(produtt)
y1 <- 0; x1 <- 0
y1[2:40] <- y[1:39]
x1[2:40] <- x[1:39]
yy <- (y-rho*y1)
xx <- (x-rho*x1)
yy[1] <- y[1]*((1-rho^2)^0.5)
xx[1] <- x[1]*((1-rho^2)^0.5)
modrh <- lm(yy~xx)
u <- residuals(modrh)
ut0 <- embed(u,2)[,1]
ut1 <- embed(u,2)[,2]
cor(ut0, ut1)
dw <- (sum((ut0-ut1)^2))/(sum(u^2))
dw
rho <- cor(ut0, ut1)
dd <- 2*(1-rho)
dd
```

### Python

```{python}
def prais_winsten(y, x, rho):
    """Transform y and x with the given rho, keeping the first observation."""
    yy = np.r_[y[0] * np.sqrt(1 - rho ** 2), y[1:] - rho * y[:-1]]
    xx = np.r_[x[0] * np.sqrt(1 - rho ** 2), x[1:] - rho * x[:-1]]
    return yy, xx

y = np.log(sal["salari"].to_numpy()); x = np.log(sal["produtt"].to_numpy())
yy, xx = prais_winsten(y, x, rho)
modrh = sm.OLS(yy, sm.add_constant(xx)).fit()
u = modrh.resid
rho = np.corrcoef(u[1:], u[:-1])[0, 1]
print(rho, durbin_watson(u), 2 * (1 - rho))
```

### SAS

```sas
/* PROC AUTOREG directly estimates the model with AR(1) errors:
   method=yw with iter re-estimates rho until convergence (Prais-Winsten) */
proc autoreg data=sal;
  model ls = lp / nlag=1 method=yw iter dw=1 dwprob;
run;
```
:::

With the small number of observations in this example, some numerical approximation must be expected. Nevertheless, note the reduction of the residual autocorrelation to 0.35 and the increase in the Durbin-Watson statistic. We iterate with a further correction, reassigning $X$ and $Y$ and repeating the same steps.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
y <- yy; x <- xx
y1 <- 0; x1 <- 0
y1[2:40] <- y[1:39]
x1[2:40] <- x[1:39]
yy <- (y-rho*y1)
xx <- (x-rho*x1)
yy[1] <- y[1]*((1-rho^2)^0.5)
xx[1] <- x[1]*((1-rho^2)^0.5)
u <- residuals(lm(yy~xx))
ut0 <- embed(u,2)[,1]
ut1 <- embed(u,2)[,2]
rho <- cor(ut0, ut1)
dw <- (sum((ut0-ut1)^2))/(sum(u^2))
rho
dw
summary(lm(yy~xx))
```

### Python

```{python}
yy, xx = prais_winsten(yy, xx, rho)
modrh2 = sm.OLS(yy, sm.add_constant(xx)).fit()
u = modrh2.resid
print(np.corrcoef(u[1:], u[:-1])[0, 1], durbin_watson(u))
print(modrh2.summary())
```

### SAS

```sas
/* with PROC AUTOREG the iteration is automatic (iter option, see above) */
```
:::

The new filtering has almost eliminated the residual autocorrelation, and indeed the Durbin-Watson test suggests accepting the null hypothesis of no autocorrelation. The last estimates shown are therefore the final ones. Finally, note that to avoid losing the first observation we used the Prais-Winsten transformation.

## 5.16 Dynamic forecasting {#sec-dynamic-forecast}

An autoregressive form in the residuals of the model can be exploited for forecasting. By appropriate substitution we have $Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}X_{t}+\rho u_{t-1}+\varepsilon_{t}$ and therefore

$$
\hat{Y}_{t+1}=\hat{\beta}_{0}+\hat{\beta}_{1}X_{t+1}+\hat{\rho}\hat{u}_{t}
\tag{5.14}
$$

This is an example of dynamic forecasting, since we take into account the errors $u$ of the previous period. The following commands compare, ex post, the static and dynamic forecasts at time $t+1$ for the log-linear model of wages on productivity, estimated over 1959-1996, for 1997.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
modf <- lm(log(salari[1:38])~log(produtt[1:38]))
modf$coeff[1]+modf$coeff[2]*log(produtt[39])
rh <- cor(embed((residuals(modf)),2))[2]
modf$coeff[1]+modf$coeff[2]*log(produtt[39])+rh*residuals(modf)[38]
log(salari)[39]
detach(sal)
```

### Python

```{python}
s38 = sal.iloc[:38]
modf = smf.ols("np.log(salari) ~ np.log(produtt)", data=s38).fit()
b0, b1 = modf.params
x39 = np.log(sal["produtt"].iloc[38])
r = modf.resid.to_numpy()
rh = np.corrcoef(r[1:], r[:-1])[0, 1]
print("static:", b0 + b1 * x39)
print("dynamic:", b0 + b1 * x39 + rh * r[-1])
print("observed:", np.log(sal["salari"].iloc[38]))
```

### SAS

```sas
/* PROC AUTOREG with AR(1) errors: the P= forecast includes the autoregressive
   component (dynamic), PM= only the structural part (static) */
data sal_prev; set sal; if _n_ > 38 then ls = .; run;
proc autoreg data=sal_prev noprint;
  model ls = lp / nlag=1 method=ml;
  output out=prev_sal p=dinamica pm=statica;
run;
proc print data=prev_sal(firstobs=39 obs=39) noobs; var anni dinamica statica; run;
```
:::

Against a known 1997 value of 4.616, the dynamic forecast (4.621) is better than the static one (4.673).

## 5.17 The RESET test {#sec-reset}

We load the data in *costo.csv* on the output level (*produz*) of a generic product, in units, and the total cost (*costo*) of the industrial process, in millions of dollars. We estimate the relationship between cost and output.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
costodf <- read.csv2("data/costo.csv")
attach(costodf)
modelloA <- lm(costo~produz)
round(modelloA$coeff, 3)
```

### Python

```{python}
costodf = pd.read_csv("data/costo.csv", sep=";", decimal=",")
modelloA = smf.ols("costo ~ produz", data=costodf).fit()
print(modelloA.params.round(3))
```

### SAS

```sas
proc import datafile="data/costo.csv" out=costodf dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
proc reg data=costodf;
  modelloA: model costo = produz;
run;
quit;
```
:::

One way of testing whether the model is correctly specified is the RESET test. In simplified form, we compare `modelloA` with `modelloB`, built by adding the squared and cubed fitted values of the dependent variable as explanatory variables, and compare the two $R^{2}$ with an $F$ test.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
costo2 <- (fitted(modelloA))^2
costo3 <- (fitted(modelloA))^3
modelloB <- lm(costo~produz+costo2+costo3)
round(modelloB$coeff, 3)
rA <- summary(modelloA)$r.squared
rB <- summary(modelloB)$r.squared
nr <- 2 # number of added regressors
nk <- 4 # number of parameters of the extended model
Fres <- ((rB-rA)/nr)/((1-rB)/(10-nk)) # 10 = number of cases
Fres
```

### Python

```{python}
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import linear_reset

costodf["costo2"] = modelloA.fittedvalues ** 2
costodf["costo3"] = modelloA.fittedvalues ** 3
modelloB = smf.ols("costo ~ produz + costo2 + costo3", data=costodf).fit()
print(modelloB.params.round(3))
Fres = ((modelloB.rsquared - modelloA.rsquared) / 2) / ((1 - modelloB.rsquared) / (10 - 4))
print(Fres)
print(linear_reset(modelloA, power=3, use_f=True))   # ready-made RESET test
```

### SAS

```sas
/* the reset option of PROC AUTOREG runs Ramsey's RESET test */
proc autoreg data=costodf;
  model costo = produz / reset;
run;
```
:::

The significance of the test statistic suggests that the original model of cost on output is misspecified.

## 5.18 The Lagrange multiplier test {#sec-lm-test}

Continuing with the same example, we use the Lagrange multiplier (LM) test to check for misspecification of the model.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
uA <- residuals(modelloA)
prod2 <- produz^2
prod3 <- produz^3
maux <- lm(uA~produz+prod2+prod3)
maux$coeff
raux <- summary(maux)$r.squared
chi <- 10*raux
chi
pchisq(chi, 2, lower.tail=FALSE)
detach(costodf)
```

### Python

```{python}
costodf["uA"] = modelloA.resid
maux = smf.ols("uA ~ produz + I(produz**2) + I(produz**3)", data=costodf).fit()
print(maux.params)
chi = 10 * maux.rsquared
print(chi, stats.chi2.sf(chi, 2))
```

### SAS

```sas
data costodf; set costodf; prod2 = produz**2; prod3 = produz**3; run;
proc reg data=costodf noprint;
  model costo = produz;
  output out=resA r=uA;
run;
proc reg data=resA outest=aux rsquare noprint;
  model uA = produz prod2 prod3;
run;
quit;
data _null_;
  set aux;
  chi = 10*_RSQ_;
  p = 1 - probchi(chi, 2);
  put chi= p=;
run;
```
:::

The degrees of freedom of the $\chi^{2}$ equal the number of restrictions of `modelloA` relative to `maux`, here 2. So the null hypothesis that the original cost-output model is correctly specified is rejected; recall, however, that this test should be used on large samples.

## 5.19 Non-nested models: the J test {#sec-j-test}

So far we have applied tests useful for choosing between two models when one is a special case of the other. If this is not the case, one can use the usual estimation statistics and diagnostics, but also a special *encompassing F test*, which specifies a new general model combining the two original models and applies the standard $F$ statistic for nested models. Another frequently used test is the Davidson-MacKinnon $J$ test, which estimates extended models by adding the fitted values of the dependent variable from the alternative models under analysis; we apply this test to the data in *conspro.csv* on per capita consumption (*cpro*) and income (*rpro*) in the United States between 1970 and 1991, in dollars.

The first model makes consumption depend on current and previous-period income; the second on current income and previous-period consumption.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
cp <- read.csv2("data/conspro.csv")
attach(cp)
rr <- embed(rpro,2)
cc <- cpro[2:22]
modA <- lm(cc~rr)
round(summary(modA)$coeff,3)
ck <- embed(cpro,2)
modB <- lm(ck[,1]~rr[,1]+ck[,2])
round(summary(modB)$coeff,3)
modAx <- lm(cc~rr+fitted(modB))
round(summary(modAx)$coeff,3)
modBx <- lm(ck[,1]~rr[,1]+ck[,2]+fitted(modA))
round(summary(modBx)$coeff,3)
detach(cp)
```

### Python

```{python}
cp = pd.read_csv("data/conspro.csv", sep=";")
d = pd.DataFrame({"c": cp["cpro"], "r": cp["rpro"],
                  "r1": cp["rpro"].shift(1), "c1": cp["cpro"].shift(1)}).dropna()
modA = smf.ols("c ~ r + r1", data=d).fit()
modB = smf.ols("c ~ r + c1", data=d).fit()
d["fitA"], d["fitB"] = modA.fittedvalues, modB.fittedvalues
modAx = smf.ols("c ~ r + r1 + fitB", data=d).fit()
modBx = smf.ols("c ~ r + c1 + fitA", data=d).fit()
for m in (modA, modB, modAx, modBx):
    print(m.summary().tables[1])
```

### SAS

```sas
proc import datafile="data/conspro.csv" out=cp dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
data cp; set cp; r1 = lag(rpro); c1 = lag(cpro); if _n_ > 1; run;
proc reg data=cp noprint;
  model cpro = rpro r1; output out=fA p=fitA;
run;
proc reg data=fA noprint;
  model cpro = rpro c1; output out=fAB p=fitB;
run;
proc reg data=fAB;
  modA:  model cpro = rpro r1;
  modB:  model cpro = rpro c1;
  modAx: model cpro = rpro r1 fitB;
  modBx: model cpro = rpro c1 fitA;
run;
quit;
```
:::

The second model might be preferred; however, the fact that the coefficient of the added regressor is significantly different from 0, with high confidence, in both estimates suggests that both original formulations are unsatisfactory, with no clear indication that one is superior to the other.

When the models are very similar, they could simply be compared using the coefficient of determination $R^{2}$, or the adjusted $R_{c}^{2}$ when the number of explanatory variables differs.

## 5.20 Information criteria: AIC and SIC {#sec-aic}

Comparing more complex models, especially when specified quite differently from one another, requires a more reliable statistic; this is the case of the *Akaike Information Criterion* (AIC) and the *Schwarz Information Criterion* (SIC).

With the usual meaning of the symbols, the first can be defined as

$$
\log AIC=(2k/n)+\log (rss/n)
\tag{5.15}
$$

and suggests choosing the model with the lowest value. For the second criterion we have

$$
\log SIC=(k/n)\log n+\log (rss/n)
\tag{5.16}
$$

and again the preferred model has the lowest value.

Let us work through an example with the previous models `modA` and `modB`.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
rssA <- sum(residuals(modA)^2)
rssB <- sum(residuals(modB)^2)
aicA <- (2*3/21)+log(rssA/21)
aicB <- (2*3/21)+log(rssB/21)
sicA <- (3/21)*log(21)+log(rssA/21)
sicB <- (3/21)*log(21)+log(rssB/21)
aicA; aicB
sicA; sicB
```

### Python

```{python}
for nome, m in (("A", modA), ("B", modB)):
    aic = 2 * 3 / 21 + np.log(m.ssr / 21)
    sic = 3 / 21 * np.log(21) + np.log(m.ssr / 21)
    print(nome, aic, sic)
# statsmodels also provides m.aic and m.bic, defined on the log-likelihood
```

### SAS

```sas
/* the aic and sbc options of PROC REG report the two criteria
   (on a different scale from the text, but ranking the models in the same way) */
proc reg data=fAB;
  modA: model cpro = rpro r1 / aic sbc;
  modB: model cpro = rpro c1 / aic sbc;
run;
quit;
```
:::

On the basis of these two criteria, model `modB` would be preferred. This is consistent with the slight superiority that emerged earlier; in particular, while the contribution of the added regressor in `modAx` is highly significant, that in `modBx` has a confidence only slightly above 95%, indicating limited additional information relative to the original specification of `modB`.
